nameStory: The Little Stint gets its name from being one of the smallest members of the sandpiper family - 'stint' is an old word meaning small or to limit in size. The scientific name Calidris minuta reinforces this theme, with 'minuta' being Latin for 'small' and 'Calidris' referring to the grey-colored waterside birds that Aristotle wrote about over 2,000 years ago.
description: The Little Stint is a tiny sandpiper that's an extremely rare visitor to New England shores, with only 19 recorded sightings in the region. This diminutive shorebird breeds in the Arctic regions of Europe and Asia, making epic migrations to winter in Africa and southern Asia. Occasionally, individuals get blown off course during migration and end up as exciting 'vagrant' birds along our Atlantic coast. It's one of the smallest sandpipers you could possibly encounter, making identification both thrilling and challenging for birdwatchers.

idTips.label: Tiny size
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller than most other sandpipers you'll see, appearing almost sparrow-sized when feeding among larger shorebirds on mudflats

idTips.label: Bill shape
idTips.description: Short, straight, thin black bill that looks almost needle-like and is perfectly proportioned to its small head

idTips.label: Leg color
idTips.description: Dark, thin legs that appear almost thread-like, helping distinguish it from similar tiny sandpipers with yellowish or pale legs

idTips.label: Breeding plumage
idTips.description: Rusty-orange wash on the face and upper breast with distinctive dark spotting, creating a warm, ruddy appearance in spring and early summer

idTips.label: Winter appearance
idTips.description: Clean grey-brown above and bright white below with a subtle pale eyebrow stripe that gives it a gentle expression

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Feeds with rapid, almost frantic pecking motions while running in short bursts across wet sand or mud, often seeming more nervous than other small sandpipers

habitat: In New England, Little Stints are most likely to appear on coastal mudflats, sandy beaches, and the edges of salt marshes, particularly during storm systems or unusual weather patterns that blow migrants off course. Look for them mixed in with flocks of other small sandpipers at places like Plum Island, Cape Cod beaches, or Connecticut's coastal refuges. They prefer areas where receding tides expose rich mudflats with tiny invertebrates to feed on.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare but most likely during May migration when birds in bright breeding plumage might appear after strong weather systems. Any sighting would be remarkable.
seasonality.summer: Virtually absent, though late summer vagrant adults in worn breeding plumage are theoretically possible in July-August during post-breeding dispersal.
seasonality.fall: Peak time for vagrant sightings, particularly September-October when juvenile birds with fresh, crisp plumage might appear among flocks of migrating sandpipers.
seasonality.winter: Essentially absent from New England, as these birds winter in tropical regions of Africa and Asia, making any winter sighting extremely noteworthy.

funFact: A Little Stint can fly over 6,000 miles non-stop during migration - that's like flying from Boston to London without landing once, all powered by a body that weighs less than a AA battery!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Least Sandpipers, but Little Stints have dark legs (not yellow-green) and a slightly different bill shape. Remember: 'Least has yellow feet, Little has dark feet.' Also distinguished from Semipalmated Sandpipers by being smaller with a thinner, more needle-like bill.
contextualKnowledge: Little Stints are considered 'Code 4' rarities in North America, meaning any sighting generates significant excitement in the birding community and should be carefully documented with photos. The bird's occurrence here represents individuals that have made a navigational error during their incredibly long migrations between Arctic breeding grounds and tropical wintering areas.
compareHints: Among its Calidris relatives in New England, Little Stint is smaller than Least Sandpiper (already our tiniest regular sandpiper) and much smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper. Unlike Least Sandpipers with their yellowish legs, Little Stint has dark legs like Semipalmated Sandpiper but with a thinner, more delicate bill. Its overall proportions appear more compact and rounded than the slightly rangier Least Sandpiper.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the Calidris sandpipers, sanderlings are notably stockier with a thicker bill than the needle-billed Least Sandpiper or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Within the Calidris genus, Semipalmated Sandpipers are most similar to Western Sandpipers but have blunter, shorter bills and less rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among its Calidris cousins, the Least Sandpiper's yellow-green legs immediately set it apart from the black-legged Semipalmated and Sanderling.

Among the Calidris sandpipers, dunlin are larger than the "peeps" (semipalmated, least, and white-rumped sandpipers) but smaller than red knot, with that diagnostic curved bill that none of the others possess.
Among the many Calidris sandpipers, Purple Sandpiper is unique for its consistently dark plumage and exclusive rocky habitat preference.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, White-rumped is most similar to Baird's Sandpiper, but Baird's lacks the white rump and has a more buff-colored breast.

Among the Calidris sandpipers in New England, pectoral sandpipers are distinguished by their larger size and that signature sharp breast line - dunlin have curved bills and different streaking, while the various 'peeps' (least, semipalmated) are much smaller.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Red Knot is the second-largest and most robust, much chunkier than Sanderling or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, the Stilt Sandpiper is the tallest and longest-legged, easily distinguished from the tiny 'peeps' like Least and Semipalmated Sandpipers.
Among the small Calidris sandpipers, Baird's stands out with its notably long wing projection past the tail - much longer than Semipalmated or Least Sandpipers.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, Buff-breasted is unique for its solid peachy-tan underparts and preference for grassy areas over mudflats.

Among New England's small sandpipers, Western Sandpipers are most easily confused with Semipalmated Sandpipers, but Westerns have longer, more drooped bill tips and often show more rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among Calidris sandpipers, Ruffs are unique in their extreme sexual size difference - much more pronounced than in Dunlin or Pectoral Sandpipers.
Among its Calidris sandpiper relatives, the Curlew Sandpiper's curved bill immediately sets it apart from straight-billed species like Sanderling and Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Compared to other small Calidris sandpipers in New England, Red-necked Stint is smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper and has darker legs than Least Sandpiper.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Sharp-tailed is most similar to Pectoral Sandpiper in size and habitat preferences, but lacks the Pectoral's sharply cut breast band.
Among Calidris sandpipers, the Surfbird is uniquely stocky and rock-adapted, unlike its beach and mudflat-loving relatives.
